reason: The passage depicts King Hezekiah responding to Assyrian insults and threats with consistent humility rather than defensiveness or pride. When confronted with harsh criticism of his military capabilities and political judgment, Hezekiah (1) acknowledges sin and submission ('I have sinned'), (2) tears his garments and covers himself in sackcloth as acts of humility, (3) seeks counsel from the prophet Isaiah rather than relying solely on his own judgment, (4) prays to God while explicitly acknowledging the power and superiority of his enemies, and (5) refuses to respond to mocking speeches with boastful counter-claims. Notably, his humble, prayerful approach—rather than prideful defiance—is presented as the correct leadership response, and the narrative rewards it with divine deliverance when God miraculously destroys the Assyrian army. The text thus implicitly models humility in the face of criticism as an effective and righteous form of leadership.
